name: Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (chronic prostatitis, NIH category III)

clinicalPearls: NIH category III prostatitis: chronic pelvic pain present for at least three of the previous six months in the absence of a demonstrable urinary tract infection
Pain is typically felt in the perineum, suprapubic area, penis, testes, or lower back, and is often accompanied by ejaculatory or post-ejaculatory discomfort
Lower urinary tract symptoms such as frequency, urgency, hesitancy, and a sense of incomplete emptying, along with sexual dysfunction, commonly coexist and reduce quality of life
Subdivided into IIIA (inflammatory, with leucocytes in expressed prostatic secretions, semen, or post-massage urine) and IIIB (non-inflammatory, with no leucocytes)
By definition standard bacterial cultures are negative, distinguishing it from acute (category I) and chronic bacterial (category II) prostatitis

Best assessed with a validated symptom score such as the NIH Chronic Prostatitis Symptom Index, and understood as a multifactorial disorder with pelvic-floor, neuropathic, and psychosocial contributions

Management is multimodal and phenotype-directed (for example the UPOINT approach) - pelvic-floor physiotherapy, neuromodulatory and analgesic strategies, alpha-blockers, and attention to anxiety or depression - rather than repeated antibiotic courses
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic pelvic pain syndrome is a heterogeneous condition with no single identifiable cause. Proposed and frequently overlapping mechanisms include an initial infective or inflammatory insult that triggers ongoing neurogenic inflammation, pelvic-floor muscle dysfunction and spasm, central sensitisation of pain pathways, autoimmune or chemical inflammation from reflux of urine into the prostatic ducts, and psychological stress that amplifies symptom perception. Because cultures are negative and the disorder spans several systems, it is best conceptualised as a chronic pain syndrome centred on the pelvis rather than a simple prostatic infection, which underpins the move away from antibiotics towards multimodal, phenotype-directed therapy.
additionalDifferentials: Benign prostatic enlargement with lower urinary tract symptoms
additionalInvestigations: Lower urinary tract localisation using pre- and post-prostatic-massage specimens (Meares-Stamey or two-glass test)
NIH Chronic Prostatitis Symptom Index questionnaire
Sexually transmitted infection screening, including urethral swab or nucleic acid amplification testing
PSA where appropriate, and cystoscopy or imaging to exclude other pathology
redFlags: PSA elevation or an abnormal prostate on examination
Systemic features suggesting acute bacterial prostatitis or a prostatic abscess
reference.prognosis: A chronic, often relapsing-remitting condition; symptoms fluctuate and can be frustrating, but many men improve substantially with a tailored multimodal programme, although a subset have persistent symptoms.
pitfalls: Prescribing repeated prolonged antibiotic courses when cultures are negative and there is no bacterial infection
Overlooking pelvic-floor muscle dysfunction and the value of physiotherapy
Ignoring the psychosocial dimension of anxiety, depression, and catastrophising that strongly influences outcome
Missing an alternative diagnosis such as bladder pain syndrome or, rarely, malignancy
references: EAU Guidelines on Chronic Pelvic Pain
management: Phenotype-directed multimodal therapy (guided by the UPOINT framework) rather than reliance on antibiotics
Alpha-adrenergic blockers to relieve lower urinary tract and voiding symptoms
Pelvic floor physiotherapy and myofascial release for pelvic-floor muscle dysfunction and spasm
Neuropathic pain agents such as tricyclic antidepressants and gabapentinoids for the pain component
A limited trial of anti-inflammatory or phytotherapeutic agents such as quercetin or pollen extract, reserving antibiotics for genuine diagnostic uncertainty
Psychological support and cognitive behavioural therapy to address stress and symptom amplification
Symptom tracking with the NIH Chronic Prostatitis Symptom Index and referral to a specialist chronic pelvic pain service for refractory cases

algorithms.title: Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (chronic prostatitis, NIH category III): Clinical Decision & Diagnostic Pathway

steps.action: NIH category III prostatitis: chronic pelvic pain present for at least three of the previous six months in the absence of a demonstrable urinary tract infection
Emergency red flag evaluation: Visible haematuria

Targeted workup: Urinalysis with mid-stream urine culture, Lower urinary tract localisation using pre- and post-prostatic-massage specimens (Meares-Stamey or two-glass test), NIH Chronic Prostatitis Symptom Index questionnaire
Targeted management: Phenotype-directed multimodal therapy (guided by the UPOINT framework) rather than reliance on antibiotics
Clinical pitfall alert: Prescribing repeated prolonged antibiotic courses when cultures are negative and there is no bacterial infection
